theme: Syllable drums: every word has beats you can clap

activities.title: Clap the beats, then tap the drums
activities.intro: Every word has beats inside it, like a little drum. Listen to the word, say it out loud with me and clap the beats, then tap the row of drums that has one drum for every clap you made.
activities.offScreen: Go and clap your own name for a grown up, one clap for every beat, and then ask them to clap their name back to you.

rounds.prompt: Rabbit. Clap it with me: rab-bit. Tap the row of drums with one drum for every clap.
Elephant. Clap it with me: el-e-phant. Tap the row of drums with one drum for every clap.
Fish. Clap it with me: fish. That one is quick. Tap the row of drums with one drum for every clap.
Caterpillar. Clap it with me: cat-er-pil-lar. That is a big one. Tap the row of drums with one drum for every clap.

activities.title: The quick pile and the long pile
activities.intro: Clap every word you hear. Some words are one clap, quick and finished. Some words are long and take three claps or more. Put the one-clap words in one pile and the long words in the other pile.
activities.offScreen: Go and find something in your house with a really long name, and clap the whole thing out for somebody.

rounds.prompt: Fish, elephant, star, butterfly. Clap each one, then put the one-clap words in one pile and the long words in the other pile.
Leaf, banana, crocodile, cup. Clap each one, then put the one-clap words in one pile and the long words in the other pile.
Caterpillar, rock, bird, alligator. Clap each one, then put the one-clap words in one pile and the long words in the other pile.
Block, umbrella, kangaroo, coin. Clap each one, then put the one-clap words in one pile and the long words in the other pile.

activities.title: Which one takes more claps
activities.intro: You will hear two words. Clap them both, one at a time, and count your claps. Then tap the word that took more claps.
activities.offScreen: Ask a grown up to say the names of two animals, and you get to decide which name takes more claps.

rounds.prompt: Cup, or butterfly? Clap them both, then tap the one that took more claps.
Elephant, or bird? Clap them both, then tap the one that took more claps.
Tiger, or caterpillar? Clap them both, then tap the one that took more claps.
Banana, or rock? Clap them both, then tap the one that took more claps.

parentCard.title: The clapping walk, and the hunt for the longest word
steps: Announce the game at the front door: today every word gets clapped, one clap for every beat. Start with the people. Clap their name, then yours, then a family member's name, then the longest name in the whole family.
Walk, and clap whatever you pass. A tree, a mailbox, a driveway, a butterfly, the neighbour's dog and then the neighbour's dog's name.

Stop somewhere and ask the why question: some words need lots of claps and some need only one. Why do you think that is? Wonder about it out loud together, let their answer be the answer, and do not tidy it up for them.

Then the hunt. Find the longest word outdoors, the one that takes the most claps, and keep it as the champion. They can try to beat the champion for the rest of the walk. Clap the champion again at the front door to see whether it still wins.
At the door, ask them to make up a brand new word that would need five claps. Nonsense words are allowed, and here the sillier the better.
notice: Do they clap the beats of the word, or do they clap along to the rhythm of your voice instead?
When a short word is said slowly and stretched out, do they hear it as more claps than it really has?
Do they start clapping words on their own after the game is over, at dinner or in the bath?
